text: The Earth moves around the Sun once every year.
The Moon moves around the Earth.
The Sun is a star at the center of our solar system.
Sunlight provides energy for most life on Earth.
The Earth rotates once every twenty-four hours.
Day and night are caused by the rotation of the Earth.
The Moon reflects light from the Sun.
Gravity keeps the planets moving around the Sun.
The solar system contains planets, moons, asteroids, and comets.
Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system.
Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun.
Venus has a very thick atmosphere.
Mars is often called the red planet.
Saturn is famous for its large system of rings.
Uranus rotates on its side compared with most other planets.
Neptune is the farthest major planet from the Sun.
A comet is made of ice, dust, and rock.
Asteroids are rocky objects that orbit the Sun.
A galaxy contains stars, gas, dust, and dark matter.
The Milky Way is the galaxy that contains our solar system.
There are billions of stars in the Milky Way.
The universe contains billions of galaxies.
Light travels extremely fast through empty space.
Light from the Sun takes about eight minutes to reach Earth.
A light-year is a measure of distance, not time.
Black holes have gravity so strong that light cannot escape from inside the event horizon.
Stars produce energy through nuclear fusion.
The Sun converts hydrogen into helium in its core.
Massive stars can explode as supernovae.
Some supernova explosions can create heavy elements.
Neutron stars are extremely dense objects.
Atoms are the basic building blocks of ordinary matter.
An atom contains protons, neutrons, and electrons.
Protons have a positive electric charge.
Electrons have a negative electric charge.
Neutrons have no electric charge.
The nucleus is located at the center of an atom.
Electrons occupy regions around the atomic nucleus.
An element is defined by the number of protons in its atoms.
Hydrogen is the simplest chemical element.
Oxygen is important for human respiration.
Carbon is a key element in living organisms.
Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen.
A water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
Water freezes at zero degrees Celsius under standard atmospheric pressure.
Water boils at one hundred degrees Celsius at standard atmospheric pressure.
Ice is less dense than liquid water.
This is why ice floats on water.
Matter can exist as a solid, liquid, gas, or plasma.
Temperature is related to the average kinetic energy of particles.
Heat naturally flows from warmer objects to cooler objects.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed in an isolated system.
Energy can change from one form into another.
Kinetic energy is the energy of motion.
Potential energy can be stored because of an object's position.
Friction converts some mechanical energy into heat.
Gravity attracts objects that have mass.
The strength of gravity depends on mass and distance.
Newton described important laws of motion and gravity.
An object at rest tends to remain at rest unless a force acts on it.
Force can change the motion of an object.
Acceleration describes how quickly velocity changes.
Speed describes how fast an object moves.
Velocity includes both speed and direction.
Sound is produced by vibrations.
Sound waves need a medium such as air, water, or solid material.
Sound cannot travel through a perfect vacuum.
Light can travel through empty space.
Different colors of visible light have different wavelengths.
Red light has a longer wavelength than blue light.
A prism can separate white light into different colors.
Plants use sunlight to produce chemical energy.
Photosynthesis takes place mainly in the leaves of plants.
Plants absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
Plants release oxygen during photosynthesis.
Animals obtain energy by consuming food.
Cells are the basic units of life.
The human body contains trillions of cells.
DNA stores genetic information in living organisms.
Genes are sections of DNA.
Proteins perform many important functions inside cells.
The human brain contains billions of neurons.
Neurons communicate using electrical and chemical signals.
The heart pumps blood through the human body.
Blood carries oxygen and nutrients to tissues.
The lungs exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide.
The skeleton supports and protects the human body.
Muscles allow the body to move.
Bacteria are microscopic living organisms.
Some bacteria are useful to humans.
Other bacteria can cause disease.
Viruses are smaller than most bacteria.
Viruses reproduce by using the machinery of host cells.
Vaccines help the immune system recognize specific pathogens.
The immune system protects the body from harmful microorganisms.
Evolution describes changes in populations over generations.
Natural selection can cause useful traits to become more common.
Living organisms inherit genetic information from their parents.
Ecosystems contain living organisms and their physical environment.
Plants are producers in many ecosystems.
Animals that eat plants are called herbivores.
Animals that eat other animals are called carnivores.
Decomposers recycle nutrients in ecosystems.
Food chains describe the transfer of energy between organisms.
Ocean water covers most of the Earth's surface.
The oceans play an important role in regulating Earth's climate.
The atmosphere is a mixture of gases surrounding the Earth.
Nitrogen is the most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere.
Oxygen makes up about one fifth of Earth's atmosphere.
Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas.
Greenhouse gases help keep the Earth warm.
Climate describes long-term patterns of weather.
Weather can change from hour to hour and day to day.
Clouds form when water vapor condenses into tiny droplets or ice crystals.
Rain is part of the Earth's water cycle.
Water evaporates from oceans, lakes, and rivers.
Water vapor can cool and form clouds.
Rivers carry water from higher ground toward lower areas.
Mountains can form when tectonic plates collide.
Earthquakes often occur near boundaries between tectonic plates.
Volcanoes can release lava, gas, and ash.
The Earth's outer shell is divided into tectonic plates.
The Earth's core is extremely hot.
Fossils provide evidence about organisms that lived in the past.
Computers process information using electronic circuits.
A computer stores information as patterns of binary digits.
A binary digit can have the value zero or one.
Computer processors perform billions of operations every second.
Software consists of instructions that tell computers what to do.
An algorithm is a sequence of steps used to solve a problem.
Artificial intelligence allows computers to perform tasks that normally require intelligence.
Machine learning allows computers to learn patterns from data.
A neural network is inspired by networks of biological neurons.
Large language models learn statistical patterns from large collections of text.
A language model predicts likely sequences of tokens.
Training changes the parameters of a neural network.
Gradient descent is commonly used to optimize neural networks.
A loss function measures how far a model's prediction is from the desired result.
More training data does not always guarantee a better model.
The quality of training data is important for machine learning.
A model can memorize training examples if it is trained improperly.
Generalization means performing well on data that was not seen during training.
Artificial intelligence does not understand the world in exactly the same way humans do.

The Earth is one of eight major planets that orbit the Sun. It takes about one year for the Earth to complete one orbit. At the same time, the Earth rotates around its own axis. This rotation causes the regular cycle of day and night.

Plants need energy to grow. Most plants obtain this energy from sunlight through a process called photosynthesis. During photosynthesis, plants use carbon dioxide and water to produce sugars. Oxygen is released as a by-product of this process.

The human brain is a complex organ made of billions of nerve cells called neurons. Neurons communicate with one another through electrical and chemical signals. Networks of neurons allow humans to learn, remember, move, and process information.

Stars are enormous spheres of hot gas. They produce energy through nuclear fusion in their cores. During fusion, light atomic nuclei combine to form heavier nuclei and release energy. The Sun uses this process to produce the light and heat that reach the Earth.

Machine learning is a field of artificial intelligence. Instead of explicitly programming every rule, developers can train a model using examples. During training, the model adjusts its parameters to reduce prediction errors. After training, the model can use the patterns it has learned to make predictions about new data.
The Sun is a star.

Earth is the third planet from the Sun. It moves around the Sun while also rotating around its own axis. Rotation produces the cycle of day and night, while Earth's orbit and axial tilt contribute to the seasons.
The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite.
The Moon does not produce its own visible light.
Moonlight is mainly sunlight reflected from the lunar surface. As the relative positions of the Sun, Earth, and Moon change, we observe different phases of the Moon.
Light travels through a vacuum at about three hundred thousand kilometers per second.
The average distance between Earth and the Sun is about one hundred and fifty million kilometers. Even across this enormous distance, sunlight reaches Earth in a little more than eight minutes.
The universe is extremely large.

The Milky Way is a galaxy containing hundreds of billions of stars. The Sun is only one of those stars, and the Milky Way itself is only one galaxy among a vast number of galaxies in the observable universe.
The color of a star is related to its surface temperature.
Hotter stars often appear bluer, while cooler stars often appear redder.

Stars can produce energy through nuclear fusion. In the Sun, hydrogen nuclei combine through a series of reactions that ultimately produce helium. Energy released by these reactions eventually escapes into space as radiation.
A black hole is an object with extremely strong gravity.
A black hole is surrounded by a boundary called the event horizon. Once something passes sufficiently far inside this boundary, it cannot return to the outside universe.
Not every star becomes a black hole.
Some massive stars may leave behind neutron stars or black holes at the end of their evolution.
Atoms are extremely small.

An ordinary atom consists of a nucleus surrounded by electrons. The nucleus contains protons and usually neutrons. Electrons occupy quantum states around the nucleus rather than following simple planetary paths.
Protons have positive electric charge.
Electrons have negative electric charge.
Neutrons have no net electric charge.
The identity of a chemical element is determined by the number of protons in its nucleus. Hydrogen has one proton, while carbon has six.
Water is an important substance for life on Earth.
A water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. Water can naturally exist on Earth as a solid, liquid, or gas, allowing it to participate in the global water cycle.
Ice usually floats on liquid water.
This happens because ordinary ice is less dense than liquid water. When water freezes, its molecules form an open crystalline structure that occupies more space.
Air is not a single substance.
Earth's atmosphere is mainly composed of nitrogen and oxygen. It also contains argon, carbon dioxide, water vapor, and smaller amounts of other gases.
Oxygen is important for respiration in many organisms.
Photosynthesis releases oxygen.
Plants can use sunlight to store energy in chemical compounds. During photosynthesis, plants use carbon dioxide and water to produce energy-rich organic molecules.
Chlorophyll absorbs certain wavelengths of visible light.
Leaves often look green because chlorophyll reflects and transmits more green light than many other visible wavelengths.
Cells are basic units of life.
Some organisms consist of only one cell, while the human body contains trillions of cells. Different cell types have specialized structures and functions.
DNA carries genetic information.
Genes are functional regions of DNA.
The DNA inside a cell contains instructions that influence how proteins are produced. These proteins participate in growth, development, metabolism, and many other biological processes.
Proteins are not only structural materials.
Many enzymes are proteins. Enzymes accelerate specific chemical reactions, allowing biological processes to occur efficiently under conditions compatible with life.
The human heart is a muscular organ.
It repeatedly contracts and relaxes to move blood through the circulatory system.
Blood transports oxygen, nutrients, hormones, and metabolic products. Hemoglobin inside red blood cells can bind oxygen and plays an important role in oxygen transport.
The lungs are major organs of respiration.
Inside the lungs, oxygen can move from tiny air spaces into the blood. Carbon dioxide moves in the opposite direction and can then leave the body during exhalation.
The brain is a major part of the nervous system.
The human brain contains billions of neurons. Neurons communicate using electrical activity and chemical signals, forming networks involved in sensation, movement, memory, language, and reasoning.
Sleep is important for human health.
The brain remains active during sleep and performs many important biological processes.
Bacteria are microscopic organisms.
Some bacteria cause disease, but many bacteria are harmless or beneficial. Bacteria participate in digestion, decomposition, nutrient cycles, and the production of foods such as yogurt.
Viruses and bacteria are different.
Viruses generally lack the complete cellular machinery required for independent reproduction. They enter host cells and use cellular components to produce new virus particles.
Antibiotics can treat certain bacterial infections.
Antibiotics do not normally cure viral infections.
Vaccines can prepare the immune system to recognize particular pathogens. When the body later encounters the pathogen, immune responses may develop more quickly and effectively.
Populations of organisms evolve.
Evolution does not mean that an individual organism deliberately changes itself. Instead, inherited characteristics in a population can change in frequency over many generations.
Genetic variation provides material for evolution.
Environmental conditions affect survival and reproduction.
Natural selection occurs when inherited differences influence reproductive success. Over many generations, traits that improve reproductive success under particular conditions may become more common.
Dinosaurs lived on Earth for a very long period.
Modern birds are evolutionarily related to certain groups of dinosaurs. Fossils, anatomy, genetics, and other forms of evidence help scientists reconstruct the history of life.
Fossils provide evidence about ancient organisms.
Only a small fraction of organisms become fossils. For this reason, the fossil record is an incomplete sample of the life that existed in the past.
Earth formed about four and a half billion years ago.
During Earth's long history, continents moved, climates changed, species appeared and disappeared, and the composition of the atmosphere evolved.
Earth's surface is not completely stationary.
The outer rocky shell of Earth is divided into tectonic plates. These plates move very slowly, but over millions of years their motion can dramatically reshape the planet.
Many earthquakes occur near plate boundaries.
Plate movement can also contribute to mountain building and volcanic activity.
A volcanic eruption may release lava, ash, rock fragments, and gases. Volcanoes can cause destructive events, but they also create new rocks and landscapes.
Weather and climate are different concepts.
Weather describes atmospheric conditions over relatively short periods. Climate describes long-term statistical patterns of temperature, rainfall, wind, and other atmospheric conditions.
Clouds consist of tiny water droplets or ice crystals.
When moist air cools sufficiently, water vapor can condense onto microscopic particles. Large collections of these droplets or crystals become visible as clouds.
Water continuously moves through Earth's environment.
Water evaporates from oceans, lakes, soil, and living organisms. It can later condense into clouds and return to the surface as rain, snow, or other forms of precipitation.
Oceans cover most of Earth's surface.
They strongly influence global climate.
Water can store large amounts of thermal energy. Ocean currents transport some of this heat around the planet and influence regional climates.
Sound is associated with vibrations.
When a sound wave travels through air, molecules undergo alternating regions of compression and rarefaction. Ordinary sound waves require matter through which to travel.
Light can travel through a vacuum.
Frequency is related to the pitch of a sound. In general, higher-frequency sound waves are perceived as having a higher pitch when they fall within the range of human hearing.
Electricity is a common physical phenomenon.
In a conducting material such as a metal, electric charges can move in response to an electric field. An organized flow of electric charge constitutes an electric current.
A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy.
A generator can convert mechanical energy into electrical energy.
Magnetic fields cannot be seen directly, but their effects can be measured through forces on magnets, magnetic materials, and moving electric charges.
Electricity and magnetism are closely connected. Changing electric and magnetic fields can propagate through space as electromagnetic waves.
Visible light is a form of electromagnetic radiation.
Radio waves, microwaves, infrared radiation, visible light, ultraviolet radiation, X-rays, and gamma rays all belong to the electromagnetic spectrum.
Energy can change from one form to another.
As an object falls, gravitational potential energy can be converted into kinetic energy. After impact, some mechanical energy may become heat, sound, or deformation.
Energy conservation is a fundamental principle of physics.
Energy does not appear from nothing or disappear without a corresponding transfer or transformation.
Forces can change motion.
When the net force acting on an object is not zero, the object's velocity can change. Acceleration describes the rate at which velocity changes.
Mass and weight are not the same thing.
Mass is an intrinsic property of an object. Weight is a force caused by gravity. An astronaut has approximately the same mass on Earth and on the Moon but has a much smaller weight on the Moon.
Satellites can orbit Earth.
An orbiting satellite is not free from gravity. Earth's gravity continually changes the direction of the satellite's velocity, causing it to follow a curved path around the planet.
Computers process information digitally.
In modern digital computers, information can ultimately be represented using patterns of zeros and ones. Text, images, audio, and video can all be encoded as numerical data.
A computer does not literally store the shape of every letter as text.
Character encoding systems assign numerical values to characters. Software can later interpret these numbers and display the corresponding symbols using fonts.
A program consists of instructions.
A processor executes instructions according to defined rules.
An algorithm is a procedure for solving a problem. Different algorithms for the same task may require very different amounts of time and memory.
The Internet is a network of networks.

When a person opens a website, data may travel through many routers and communication links before reaching the destination. Information is often divided into packets that are transmitted and later reassembled.
Artificial intelligence includes many different methods.
Machine learning is an important branch of artificial intelligence. Instead of explicitly programming every rule, developers can allow a model to adjust its parameters by learning from data.
A neural network contains many numerical parameters.
Before training, these parameters are often initialized with small random values. During training, examples are processed, errors are measured, and optimization algorithms adjust the parameters.
A language model can have a surprisingly simple objective.
For example, a model can learn to predict the next token based on previous tokens. By repeating this task across enormous amounts of text, the model can learn many statistical patterns of language.
A tokenizer connects text with a language model.
The tokenizer converts text into a sequence of tokens. Each token receives an integer identifier, which is then transformed into numerical vectors before being processed by the neural network.
A text model does not initially know what the word "apple" means.
At first, the token is only a numerical symbol. By observing the contexts in which the token appears, the model gradually develops internal representations associated with its usage.
Embeddings represent tokens as vectors.
Tokens that occur in related contexts may develop representations that reflect some of their statistical relationships, although these representations do not function exactly like human concepts.
Training a neural network requires an objective.
A loss function measures how different the model's predictions are from desired outputs. Optimization methods use information from the loss to modify the model parameters.
Backpropagation is an important training algorithm.
It efficiently calculates how changes in model parameters would affect the loss. An optimizer can then use these gradients to update the parameters.
More training is not always better.
If a model repeatedly sees a small training set, it may begin to memorize specific examples instead of learning patterns that generalize to new data.
This problem is known as overfitting.
A model may have very low training loss while performing poorly on unseen examples. A validation set helps researchers detect when this begins to happen.
Training data quality matters.
Large amounts of duplicated, incorrect, or poorly written text can teach undesirable patterns. Increasing the number of tokens alone does not guarantee a better model.
Scientific knowledge depends on evidence.

Scientists propose explanations and test them using observations, measurements, experiments, and mathematical reasoning. Results that disagree with a hypothesis can be just as informative as results that support it.
Science is a process rather than a collection of permanent facts.

New evidence can strengthen an existing theory, reveal its limitations, or lead researchers toward a better explanation. The ability to revise ideas in response to evidence is one of the strengths of scientific reasoning.
Measurement always has some uncertainty.
No physical measurement is infinitely precise. Scientists estimate uncertainty so that results can be interpreted and compared appropriately.
Models are simplified representations of reality.
A scientific model does not need to contain every detail of a system. A useful model captures the features that are important for answering a particular question.
Mathematics is widely used in science.
Equations allow scientists to describe relationships precisely, make quantitative predictions, and compare theoretical ideas with experimental observations.
Probability helps describe uncertainty.

Some processes are difficult to predict because information is incomplete, while other physical processes contain randomness at a fundamental level. Probability provides a mathematical framework for reasoning about uncertain outcomes.
Data alone does not automatically produce knowledge.

Measurements must be interpreted using models, assumptions, statistical methods, and existing evidence. Good scientific reasoning requires understanding both what the data shows and what it does not show.
Mathematics studies abstract patterns involving quantity, structure, space, and change.
Natural numbers can represent counting and order.
A prime number has exactly two positive divisors: one and itself.
Two is the only even prime number.
Every integer greater than one has a unique prime factorization apart from the order of the factors.
An irrational number cannot be expressed as a ratio of two integers.
Pi is an irrational number equal to the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter.
A function describes a relationship between inputs and outputs.
A derivative describes an instantaneous rate of change.
An integral can represent accumulated quantities such as area, distance, or total mass.
Probability provides a mathematical language for uncertainty.
Conditional probability describes the probability of an event given that another condition is known.
Bayes' theorem combines prior information with new evidence to update probabilities.
Statistics is concerned with collecting, describing, analyzing, and interpreting data.
The mean can be strongly affected by extreme values, while the median is often more resistant.
Standard deviation measures how widely values are spread around their mean.
Correlation does not by itself establish causation.
Random sampling can reduce systematic bias in how observations are selected.
Matrices can represent systems of linear relationships and are widely used in graphics and machine learning.
A vector can represent both magnitude and direction.
Coordinate systems provide numerical descriptions of position in space.
Geometry studies shapes, sizes, positions, and spatial relationships.
Symmetry is important in mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology.
Fractals can display similar geometric structure across different scales.
A chaotic system can follow deterministic equations while remaining extremely sensitive to its initial conditions.
Entropy is an important state quantity in thermodynamics.
In an isolated system, spontaneous processes generally proceed in a direction that does not decrease total entropy.
Thermal equilibrium occurs when there is no net heat transfer between systems in contact.
During a phase transition, a substance can absorb or release latent heat without a large change in temperature.
Evaporation occurs at a liquid surface, while boiling occurs throughout the liquid once suitable conditions are reached.
Surface tension arises because molecules at a liquid surface experience different forces from molecules in the interior.
Capillary action depends on surface tension and interactions between a liquid and a solid surface.
Density is mass per unit volume.
Whether an object floats depends on gravity, buoyancy, and the densities of the object and surrounding fluid.
Archimedes' principle states that buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced fluid.
A wave can transfer energy without transporting the surrounding material over the same long distance.
Wavelength is the spatial distance between neighboring points at the same phase.
Frequency measures how many oscillations occur per unit time.
For a wave traveling at a fixed speed, higher frequency corresponds to shorter wavelength.
Waves can add together when they overlap.
Interference results from the superposition of waves.
Diffraction occurs when waves spread after passing through an opening or around an obstacle.
Polarization describes the orientation of oscillations in a transverse wave.
Light usually changes speed when it enters a material with a different refractive index.
Refraction is the change in direction that can occur when light passes between different media.
A converging lens can bring parallel rays toward a focus.
A diverging lens causes parallel rays to spread apart.
Microscopes use optical systems to enlarge images of small objects.
Telescopes collect light from distant objects and form images for observation.
Electrical resistance describes opposition to electric current.
Under suitable conditions, current is proportional to voltage and inversely proportional to resistance.
Components connected in series carry the same current through each component.
Branches connected in parallel have the same voltage across their endpoints.
Electrical power measures the rate at which electrical energy is transferred or converted.
A capacitor stores energy in an electric field.
An inductor stores energy associated with a magnetic field.
Alternating current changes direction periodically.
Transformers use electromagnetic induction to change alternating voltages.
Electromagnetic induction occurs when a changing magnetic flux produces an electromotive force.
Semiconductors have electrical properties between those of typical conductors and insulators.
Doping can modify the electrical behavior of a semiconductor.
A diode generally allows current to flow more easily in one direction than the other.
A transistor can act as an electronic switch or an amplifier.
Modern processors contain enormous numbers of transistors.
Quantum mechanics describes physical behavior on atomic and subatomic scales.
The state of a quantum system can be represented by a wavefunction or related mathematical description.
Quantum measurements are often predicted in terms of probabilities.
Light displays wave behavior and can also exchange energy in discrete packets called photons.
Electrons also exhibit wave-like and particle-like behavior.
The uncertainty principle limits how precisely certain pairs of physical quantities can be specified together.
Electrons in atoms occupy allowed quantum energy states.
Atoms can absorb or emit particular amounts of energy when electrons change between allowed states.
Lasers can produce highly directional and coherent light.
Relativity changed scientific ideas about space, time, energy, and gravity.
Special relativity states that the speed of light in vacuum is the same for all inertial observers.
At speeds close to the speed of light, measurements of time and distance show relativistic effects.
Mass and energy are deeply related.
General relativity describes gravity through the geometry of spacetime and the distribution of matter and energy.
Gravitational waves are propagating disturbances in spacetime curvature.
Cosmic expansion means that the average separation between distant galaxies increases with time.
Astronomical redshift helps scientists study the expansion of the universe.
The cosmic microwave background is ancient radiation left from the early universe.
Dark matter does not emit much ordinary light, but its gravitational effects influence galaxies and gravitational lensing.
An exoplanet is a planet that orbits a star other than the Sun.
The transit method can detect some exoplanets by measuring periodic decreases in a star's brightness.
A pulsar is a rapidly rotating neutron star that produces regular pulses of electromagnetic radiation.
A star's mass strongly influences how it evolves.
Some elements up to iron can be produced through fusion processes inside stars.
Many elements heavier than iron require more extreme astrophysical processes for their formation.
Chemical bonds arise from electron distributions and quantum interactions between atoms.
A covalent bond commonly involves the sharing of electrons between atoms.
An ionic bond is associated with electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
Metallic bonding helps explain the conductivity and malleability of many metals.
The periodic table arranges chemical elements by atomic number.
Elements in the same group often have related valence-electron structures and similar chemical behavior.
A solution contains one or more solutes dispersed in a solvent.
Concentration measures the amount of solute in a specified amount of solution or solvent.
A saturated solution cannot dissolve additional solute under the same conditions.
Solubility can depend on temperature, pressure, and the chemical nature of the substances.
In the Brønsted-Lowry model, acids donate protons and bases accept protons.
The pH scale is commonly used to describe the acidity of aqueous solutions.
Redox reactions involve electron transfer or changes in oxidation state.
Electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive certain nonspontaneous chemical reactions.
A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
Polymers are large molecules built from many linked repeating or related molecular units.
Plastics, rubber, proteins, and DNA can all be studied as macromolecular materials.
The cell membrane contains lipids and proteins that regulate movement of substances into and out of the cell.
Mitochondria participate in energy conversion in many eukaryotic cells.
Ribosomes build proteins according to genetic instructions.
Chromosomes are structures made of DNA and associated proteins.
Human body cells usually contain chromosomes in pairs.
Meiosis produces reproductive cells with half the usual chromosome number.
A genetic mutation is a change in a DNA sequence.
Mutations can be neutral, harmful, or beneficial depending on their effects and environment.
A phenotype is influenced by both genetic and environmental factors.
Gene expression controls when, where, and how strongly genetic information is used.
Stem cells can self-renew and can differentiate into other cell types under suitable conditions.
Neurotransmitters are chemical messengers used by nervous systems.
A synapse is a junction where a neuron communicates with another cell.
Learning can be accompanied by changes in the strength and activity of neural connections.
The hippocampus is important for several forms of memory formation.
The cerebellum contributes to coordination, balance, and motor learning.
The kidneys filter blood and regulate water, salts, and acid-base balance.
The liver participates in metabolism, detoxification, storage, and synthesis of many important molecules.
The pancreas has digestive functions and also produces hormones involved in blood glucose regulation.
Hormones are chemical signals that coordinate processes in different parts of the body.
The human microbiome includes microorganisms living on and inside the body.
The composition of the microbiome can be influenced by diet, environment, medication, and age.
The immune system includes rapid innate defenses and highly specific adaptive responses.
Antibodies can recognize particular molecular structures called antigens.
Allergies occur when the immune system overreacts to substances that are usually harmless.
Cell division is tightly regulated, and loss of this regulation can contribute to cancer.
Cancer is not one disease but a large group of diseases involving abnormal cell growth and spread.
Microorganisms can use fermentation to produce acids, alcohols, and other metabolic products.
Yeasts are fungi, and some species are widely used in baking and food fermentation.
Fungi form a biological kingdom distinct from plants and animals.
Lichens are stable partnerships involving fungi and photosynthetic organisms such as algae or cyanobacteria.
Most salts in seawater ultimately come from weathering of rocks and geological processes.
Ocean salinity varies from one region to another.
Earth's rotation produces Coriolis effects in large-scale atmospheric and oceanic motion.
The ozone layer absorbs much of the Sun's high-energy ultraviolet radiation.
The troposphere is the lowest major layer of the atmosphere and contains most weather.
The stratosphere lies above the troposphere and contains the region of highest ozone concentration.
Wind is air moving relative to Earth's surface and is strongly influenced by pressure differences.
Different rates of heating over land and water can produce local sea breezes and land breezes.
Lightning rapidly heats nearby air, causing expansion that produces thunder.
Earth's magnetic field deflects some charged particles arriving from the Sun.
Auroras result from interactions among solar particles, Earth's magnetic field, and the upper atmosphere.
Tectonic plates usually move only a few centimeters per year.
Mid-ocean ridges are major regions where new oceanic crust forms.
At a subduction zone, one tectonic plate descends beneath another.
Seismic waves allow scientists to infer the structure of Earth's interior.
P waves can travel through solids and liquids, while S waves cannot travel through liquids.
A central processing unit executes instructions and performs many calculations.
A cache stores frequently used data close to a processor to reduce access delay.
Random-access memory normally loses its stored contents when electrical power is removed.
An operating system manages processors, memory, storage devices, and peripheral hardware.
A file system defines how data is organized, named, stored, and retrieved.
A database stores and manages information in a structured way.
Database indexes can speed up some queries at the cost of additional storage and update work.
Compression algorithms reduce storage or transmission requirements by removing redundancy.
Lossless compression can reconstruct the original data exactly.
Lossy compression discards some information to achieve higher compression ratios.
A checksum can help detect certain errors introduced during storage or transmission.
Error-correcting codes add redundancy so that some data errors can be detected and repaired.
Internet protocols define how devices address, package, route, and deliver data.
The Domain Name System maps human-readable domain names to network address information.
Encryption transforms readable information so that only authorized parties with suitable keys can recover it.
A hash function maps input data of arbitrary length to a fixed-length digest.
A cryptographic hash function should make it computationally difficult to reconstruct the original input from the digest.
Public-key cryptography uses mathematically related keys with different roles.
Digital signatures can verify message origin and detect unauthorized modification.
A training set is used to fit model parameters, while a validation set helps choose models and hyperparameters.
Cross-validation can estimate generalization more efficiently when data is limited.
Regularization reduces overfitting by discouraging excessive model complexity.
The learning rate controls the size of parameter updates during optimization.
Batch size affects training speed, memory use, and the noise in gradient estimates.
Attention mechanisms allow a model to assign different importance to different input positions.
Positional information helps a model distinguish the order and relative location of tokens.
Pretraining learns broad patterns from large datasets, while fine-tuning adapts a model to more specific tasks.
A control group provides a comparison baseline in an experiment.
Double-blind experimental designs can reduce bias caused by expectations of participants and researchers.
Replication helps determine whether a scientific result is robust.
Peer review is one method the scientific community uses to evaluate methods, evidence, and conclusions.
Measurement error can arise from instrument limitations, sampling, procedure, or model assumptions.
Significant figures communicate an appropriate level of precision in measured quantities.
A useful scientific theory explains existing evidence and makes predictions that can be tested.

When a function is continuous at a point, inputs sufficiently close to that point produce outputs close to the function value there. Continuity connects local limits with actual function values and is a key condition behind many theorems in calculus.

A random variable maps outcomes of a random experiment to numerical values. A probability distribution describes how likely those values are, while expectation and variance summarize long-run average behavior and variability. Different distributions model different kinds of random processes.

Quantum entanglement occurs when the joint state of multiple quantum systems cannot be separated into independent states. Measurements on entangled particles can show strong correlations, but those correlations cannot be used to transmit controllable information faster than light.

Chemical equilibrium is a dynamic state. Forward and reverse reactions continue, but at equal rates, so the macroscopic composition remains stable. Changing temperature or concentration can cause the system to establish a new equilibrium.

Cells coordinate energy production and biosynthesis through metabolic networks. Glucose, fatty acids, and amino acids can enter shared metabolic pathways through different routes, while hormones and enzyme activities regulate those pathways according to physiological conditions.

Ocean circulation transports heat from one region to another. Surface circulation is strongly influenced by winds and Earth's rotation, while deep circulation also depends on density differences caused by temperature and salinity. The ocean is therefore a major component of the global climate system.

An operating system manages computer resources through mechanisms such as processes, virtual memory, and file systems. It must let multiple programs share processors and memory efficiently while isolating failures so that one application does not damage the entire system.

A distributed system cannot assume that the network is always reliable. Requests may be delayed, duplicated, or lost, and remote machines may fail during execution. Retries, idempotency, replication, and consistency protocols are therefore central to reliable service design.

Correlation describes a statistical association between variables, but it does not by itself establish causation. To determine whether intervening on one variable changes another, researchers must consider confounding factors, study design, and reasonable assumptions about how the data were generated.

A test set should remain as independent as possible and be used only for final evaluation on unseen data. If a model is repeatedly modified in response to test results, the test set gradually becomes part of the development process and the reported score can overestimate true generalization.
A sequence is an ordered list of numbers indexed by integers. Convergence concerns its long-run behavior: as the index grows, the terms must become arbitrarily close to a fixed value.

The first few terms of a sequence do not determine whether it converges. A sequence may fluctuate early and still approach a limit if all sufficiently late terms remain as close to that value as required.
An infinite series adds the terms of a sequence through its partial sums. Terms approaching zero are necessary for many convergent series, but that condition alone is not sufficient.
Infinite series can approximate complicated functions with a finite number of terms. The approximation is useful only when the convergence region and the size of the omitted remainder are understood.

A multivariable function depends on several inputs at once. The influence of one variable can depend on the current values of the others, so its behavior cannot always be understood one coordinate at a time.

A partial derivative measures local change with respect to one variable while the others are held fixed. The gradient combines these derivatives and points in the direction of steepest local increase.

Optimization searches for the best feasible choice according to an objective such as minimum cost or maximum efficiency. Finding a locally good point does not automatically prove that it is globally optimal.
Constraints define which candidate solutions are allowed. A solution that looks ideal without restrictions may become impossible once limits on resources, capacity, or safety are included.

A differential equation relates an unknown function to one or more of its rates of change. With suitable initial conditions, it can describe how quantities such as temperature, velocity, or concentration evolve over time.

The same differential equation can produce very different trajectories under different initial conditions. A useful model therefore specifies both the evolution law and the meaning of its parameters and starting state.
Combinatorics studies how many ways finite objects can be selected, arranged, or connected. Product rules, case splits, and recurrences often replace impractical brute-force enumeration.
A common counting error is to count the same outcome more than once. Before choosing a formula, it is important to decide whether order matters and whether an object may be selected repeatedly.
Graph theory represents entities as vertices and relationships as edges. Road systems, social connections, and software dependencies can all be modeled this way and analyzed with common algorithms.

A shortest path is defined by edge weights rather than by geometric appearance. If the weights represent time, cost, or risk instead of distance, the optimal route can change even though the graph structure stays the same.
A Markov chain models random transitions between states under the assumption that the next-step distribution depends on the current state rather than on the full earlier history.

Some Markov chains approach a stationary distribution over time, making long-run proportions largely independent of the starting state. This behavior is not automatic and depends on structural conditions of the chain.
A statistic varies from sample to sample even when the underlying population is fixed. The distribution of a statistic across repeated samples is called its sampling distribution.

Larger samples often reduce the random variability of an estimator. Standard error describes the typical sampling variation of an estimate and should not be confused with the standard deviation of individual observations.

A regression model predicts or explains an outcome using one or more variables, but predictions rarely match every observation exactly. The difference between an observed and fitted value is a residual.

Residual patterns can reveal structure that a model has missed. Curvature, clustering, or changing spread in residual plots may indicate that some assumptions of a simple regression are inappropriate.

Angular momentum describes rotational motion and depends on mass distribution, the chosen axis, and rotational velocity. In a system with negligible external torque, total angular momentum is conserved.

A spinning skater can rotate faster by pulling the arms inward. Bringing mass closer to the axis reduces rotational inertia, so angular velocity increases while angular momentum remains approximately constant.

Simple harmonic motion occurs when the restoring force is proportional to displacement from equilibrium and points back toward equilibrium. Ideal springs and small-angle pendulums can approximate this behavior.

In simple harmonic motion, displacement varies periodically while speed is greatest near equilibrium. Real oscillators usually experience damping, so their amplitude decreases as energy is dissipated.

Pressure in a stationary fluid increases with depth because deeper points support more fluid above them. For a uniform fluid, pressure differences depend mainly on density, gravity, and height difference.

Hydraulic devices transmit pressure through a confined fluid. Different piston areas can trade force for displacement, but the energy balance prevents the device from creating mechanical work from nothing.

For ideal steady flow, pressure, speed, and elevation can be related through a mechanical-energy balance. Faster flow is often associated with lower static pressure along a streamline under the required assumptions.
Bernoulli's relation is an energy statement for fluids. Real pipes dissipate mechanical energy through friction and other losses, so engineering models usually include additional loss terms.

Specific heat capacity measures the energy required to raise the temperature of a unit mass by one degree. Materials with different heat capacities can undergo very different temperature changes after absorbing the same energy.

Water has a relatively high heat capacity, allowing it to store substantial thermal energy with modest temperature change. This matters in climate, biological temperature regulation, and industrial cooling.

Most materials expand when heated because increasing thermal motion changes average atomic or molecular spacing. Bridges and rails include expansion allowances to prevent large stresses during temperature changes.
Materials have different thermal expansion coefficients. When two bonded materials are heated together, their unequal preferred expansions can create bending or internal stress.
Electric potential is potential energy per unit charge. A potential difference determines how much electrical energy can be transferred when charge moves between two locations.
The electric field is a vector describing force per unit charge, while electric potential is a scalar. In many problems, adding scalar potentials is simpler than adding field vectors directly.
A capacitor stores energy in an electric field by separating charge. Capacitance relates stored charge to voltage and depends on geometry and the dielectric material between conductors.
Combining capacitors with resistors creates charging and discharging behavior with a characteristic time scale. Such circuits are used for filtering, timing, and signal conditioning.

A changing magnetic flux through a circuit produces an induced electromotive force. The change can come from varying field strength, changing loop area, or relative motion between the field and the loop.

Electric generators use electromagnetic induction to convert mechanical energy into electrical energy. Rotating coils or magnets changes magnetic flux continuously and produces a time-varying voltage.
Optical resolution is limited by wavelength and aperture. Even a perfect lens produces a diffraction pattern of finite width rather than an infinitely sharp image of a point source.
Shorter wavelengths and larger effective apertures improve conventional angular resolution. Large astronomical telescopes are valuable both for collecting more light and for resolving finer detail.
Stoichiometry follows from conservation of atoms in a balanced chemical equation. Coefficients specify mole ratios among reactants and products rather than direct mass ratios.
Real reactions often contain a limiting reactant. Once that reactant is consumed, it sets the maximum amount of product that can form even if other reactants remain.

Molar concentration expresses the amount of solute in moles per unit volume of solution. During dilution without solute loss, the amount of solute stays constant while concentration decreases as volume increases.

Concentration is an important experimental control variable. Equal volumes of solutions can contain very different numbers of solute particles if their concentrations differ, affecting reaction rates and stoichiometric outcomes.

Acid strength describes the tendency to donate protons in a given solvent, whereas acid concentration describes how much acid is present. A strong acid can be dilute, and a weak acid can be concentrated.
A weak acid ionizes only partially in water, leaving both neutral molecules and ions in solution. An equilibrium constant can quantify the extent of ionization and compare weak acids.
Redox reactions involve electron transfer or changes in oxidation state. Oxidation and reduction occur together, so the electron loss in one half-reaction must match electron gain in another.

Combustion, battery discharge, and metal corrosion can all be analyzed as redox processes. Their visible behavior differs, but each involves redistribution of electrons and accompanying energy changes.

Even a sparingly soluble salt releases a small concentration of ions into water. A solubility-product relation describes the equilibrium combination of those ion concentrations in a saturated solution.
Adding a source of an ion already present in a sparingly soluble salt can shift the equilibrium toward the solid. This common-ion effect is useful for controlling precipitation and separation.

Reaction order describes the mathematical dependence of reaction rate on reactant concentrations. It is determined experimentally and cannot in general be read directly from the overall balanced equation.
Changing a reactant concentration and measuring the resulting rate can reveal a rate law. That law constrains possible mechanisms, although it rarely proves a unique microscopic pathway by itself.

Many chemical reactions must cross an energy barrier before products can form. This barrier is described by activation energy, so even an overall energy-releasing reaction may need an initial energy input.
Raising temperature increases the fraction of particles energetic enough to cross the barrier. A catalyst accelerates a reaction by providing a pathway with a lower effective activation energy.

Functional groups strongly influence the reactivity of organic molecules. Hydroxyl, carbonyl, carboxyl, and amino groups affect polarity, acid-base behavior, and the types of reactions a molecule tends to undergo.

Molecules with similar carbon skeletons can have very different solubility or biological behavior when their functional groups differ. Organic chemistry therefore depends on connectivity as well as elemental composition.

Polymers consist of many linked molecular units, but chain length, branching, and interactions between chains strongly influence bulk properties. The same monomer can produce materials with different behavior under different polymerization conditions.
Thermoplastics can often soften and be reshaped when heated, whereas highly cross-linked thermosets do not readily melt again. The difference arises from how polymer chains are connected.

Many chemical processes occur primarily at surfaces because reactants encounter the outermost atoms first. Increasing a solid's specific surface area often increases the number of available adsorption or reaction sites.
Catalyst particles are often made porous to expose more active sites. Small changes in surface composition or crystal face can substantially alter catalytic activity and selectivity.

The cell membrane is a selective barrier made largely of lipids and proteins. Different molecules cross it through different mechanisms, allowing the cell to maintain an internal environment distinct from its surroundings.

Active transport uses energy to move substances against an electrochemical gradient, whereas passive transport follows existing gradients. Together these processes shape the distribution of ions and nutrients.
Mitochondria convert part of the chemical energy in nutrients into ATP that cells can readily use. This conversion occurs through a sequence of coupled reactions rather than one single step.

Electron transfer across the inner mitochondrial membrane helps build a proton gradient. ATP synthase uses that gradient to make ATP, so energy conversion depends on maintaining an unequal distribution across the membrane.

The cell cycle organizes growth, DNA replication, and division into coordinated stages. Checkpoints use information about DNA integrity and replication status to determine whether a cell should proceed.
Loss of cell-cycle control can allow damaged cells to keep dividing. Cancer generally develops through multiple changes in regulatory pathways rather than from one ordinary cell division event.

Meiosis produces reproductive cells with half the usual chromosome number. Homologous chromosomes can exchange corresponding DNA segments during the process, creating new combinations of genetic material.
Independent assortment and recombination both increase genetic variation. Different gametes from the same individual therefore usually contain different combinations of parental alleles.
Possessing a gene does not mean that a cell expresses it continuously. Transcription factors, chromatin state, and cellular signals help determine when, where, and how strongly a gene is used.
Different body-cell types usually contain essentially the same genome yet perform different functions. One major reason is that they activate different subsets of genes.

A newly synthesized protein must usually adopt an appropriate three-dimensional structure to function. Its amino-acid sequence shapes folding, while the cellular environment and molecular chaperones can influence the final structure.
Misfolded proteins may lose normal function or form harmful aggregates. Cells therefore maintain quality-control systems that refold, isolate, or degrade abnormal proteins.

Homeostasis keeps internal conditions within workable ranges rather than holding every variable perfectly constant. Temperature, blood glucose, and pH all fluctuate while regulatory systems continually respond.
Negative feedback is a common homeostatic mechanism. When a regulated variable moves away from its target range, the response acts in the opposite direction and tends to bring the variable back.
Population genetics studies how allele frequencies change across generations. Selection, random drift, mutation, and migration can all alter the genetic composition of a population.

Genetic drift is especially strong in small populations because each generation is a limited sample of the previous one. An allele can become common or disappear by chance even without a selective advantage.
Real ecosystems are usually food webs rather than single food chains. A change in one population can influence many others through both direct feeding relationships and indirect pathways.

Ecological stability depends on interaction strengths, environmental variation, and resource limits. Greater diversity does not guarantee stability, although multiple pathways can sometimes provide functional alternatives.
The human microbiome can process dietary compounds that human enzymes do not fully break down and can produce metabolites that interact with intestinal cells, immune pathways, and other organs.
Microbiome composition changes with diet, medication, age, and environment. An association between a microbe and a health condition does not by itself establish that the microbe causes the condition.

Plate boundaries include divergent, convergent, and transform settings, each associated with different geological processes. New oceanic crust forms at many ridges, while subduction returns older oceanic lithosphere toward the mantle.
Earthquakes are common near many plate boundaries, but their depth and fault mechanisms vary with tectonic setting. Seismic waves help scientists infer both fault motion and deeper Earth structure.

Igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks are connected through the rock cycle. Melting, cooling, weathering, deposition, burial, and heating can transform one rock type into another over geologic time.
A rock's present classification records only part of its history. Continued burial, uplift, erosion, or melting can move the same material into a very different geological process.
Soil formation depends on parent material, climate, organisms, topography, and time. Weathering supplies mineral particles while plants, microbes, and animals add and transform organic matter.

Soils are vertically structured rather than uniform. Moving water can remove substances from upper horizons and accumulate them deeper down, allowing a soil profile to record long-term environmental processes.

Uneven solar heating creates temperature and density differences that drive rising and sinking air. Convection redistributes heat, moisture, and momentum vertically and is central to many weather processes.
Warm moist air cools as it rises and expands. Once saturation is reached, condensation can release latent heat, altering buoyancy and feeding back on the development of clouds and storms.

Jet streams are narrow bands of fast winds in the upper troposphere. Their location and strength are linked to large-scale temperature contrasts and Earth's rotation, and they influence the paths of weather systems.
A jet stream is not a stationary straight line. It meanders in large waves whose shape can alter exchanges of warm and cold air and influence midlatitude weather patterns.
Earth's long-term climate depends on the balance between absorbed solar energy and infrared energy emitted to space. A persistent change in this balance can drive an adjustment in global temperature.

Clouds, ice, aerosols, and greenhouse gases all influence the planetary energy budget in different ways. Some mainly alter reflected sunlight, while others strongly affect outgoing infrared radiation.
Ocean upwelling brings deeper water toward the surface. That water is often rich in nutrients, supporting phytoplankton growth and contributing to productive fisheries.

Coastal upwelling often results from winds acting together with Earth's rotation. When surface water moves away from the coast, deeper water rises to replace it, with strength varying by season and climate state.

The carbon cycle contains reservoirs in the atmosphere, ocean, soils, living organisms, and rocks. Carbon moves among them on very different time scales, from rapid photosynthesis to extremely slow geological processes.
Changes in atmospheric carbon dioxide depend on both sources and sinks. Oceans and land ecosystems absorb part of added carbon, but the strength of those sinks is not fixed over time.

Remote sensing uses sensors on satellites or aircraft to observe Earth's surface and atmosphere without direct contact. Different wavelength bands respond differently to vegetation, water, clouds, and temperature.

A pixel value in a remote-sensing image is not automatically the physical quantity of interest. Calibration, correction, and retrieval models are needed to convert measured radiation into useful environmental variables.

Earthquake magnitude and intensity describe different quantities. Magnitude characterizes the size of the source event, whereas intensity describes the shaking and damage experienced at a particular location.
A single earthquake has one source magnitude estimate, but intensity varies from place to place. Distance, local geology, and building characteristics all influence the effects observed locally.
Stars form in dense regions of cold molecular clouds. When gravity overcomes internal pressure and other support, gas contracts and a protostar grows hotter and denser.
A protostar does not immediately become a stable star. It enters the long-lived main-sequence stage only after its core becomes hot and dense enough for sustained hydrogen fusion.
A star's lifetime depends strongly on its mass. Massive stars contain more fuel, but their hotter cores consume that fuel much faster, so they usually live for less time than low-mass stars.
Stars near the Sun's mass can remain stable for billions of years, while very massive stars evolve much more quickly. Mass influences luminosity, internal structure, and eventual fate.

A white dwarf is a dense stellar remnant left by many low- and intermediate-mass stars. It is supported against further collapse mainly by electron degeneracy pressure rather than ongoing core fusion.
Newly formed white dwarfs are hot, but they lack a major continuing fusion source. They therefore cool and fade gradually over extremely long time scales.
Measuring the orbital speeds of stars and gas in a galaxy helps infer how mass is distributed. In many galaxies, outer material moves faster than expected from visible matter alone.

Galaxy rotation curves are one line of evidence for dark matter, but not the only one. Motions in galaxy clusters, gravitational lensing, and large-scale cosmic structure provide additional constraints.
Massive objects curve spacetime and therefore deflect light passing nearby. This gravitational-lensing effect can alter the apparent position and shape of more distant sources.

Strong lensing can create multiple images, arcs, or nearly complete rings, while weak lensing produces subtle distortions. Combining many weak-lensing measurements can map otherwise invisible mass distributions.
Cosmic expansion means that average separations between distant, unbound galaxies grow with time. It is not simply an explosion of matter outward from a central point into preexisting static space.
Locally bound systems do not expand in proportion with the universe. Structures such as the solar system and individual galaxies are dominated by their own gravitational binding.

The cosmic microwave background is nearly uniform radiation left from the early universe. It comes from the era when the universe cooled enough for neutral atoms to form and photons to travel freely over large distances.

Tiny temperature variations in the microwave background trace early density differences. Gravitational growth over billions of years connected those small variations to the later formation of galaxies and large-scale structure.
When an exoplanet passes in front of its star, the observed stellar brightness can decrease slightly. Repeated dips help estimate the planet's orbital period and its size relative to the star.

The transit method has a geometric selection effect because transits are easiest to see when an orbit is aligned close to our line of sight. Detected planets therefore are not an unbiased sample of all planets in the galaxy.
A black hole itself does not emit light from inside its event horizon, but infalling matter can form a hot accretion disk outside the horizon and produce intense radiation.

Accretion can convert gravitational potential energy into heat and radiation very efficiently. Some active galactic nuclei powered by black-hole accretion can outshine the ordinary stars of their host galaxies.

Accelerating asymmetric mass distributions can generate gravitational waves that propagate as disturbances of spacetime. Merging black holes or neutron stars can produce signals detectable by modern instruments.

Gravitational-wave detectors measure extremely small relative changes in length. Observations from multiple detectors help determine source direction and reduce the chance of mistaking local noise for an astrophysical event.
A hash table maps keys to storage locations using a hash function, enabling fast average-case lookup and update. Different keys can map to the same location, so collisions must be handled explicitly.
Hash-table performance depends on more than the hash function. Load factor and resizing policy matter because a crowded table increases collisions and can make normally fast operations much slower.
Sorting algorithms rearrange data into an ordered sequence. They differ in time complexity, extra memory use, stability, and suitability for data that does not fit entirely in memory.
No sorting algorithm is best in every setting. Data size, existing order, comparison cost, and memory limits all influence which method performs well in practice.
Computer storage is organized as a hierarchy: registers and caches are fast but small, main memory is larger and slower, and persistent storage is larger still with much higher access latency.
Program performance is often limited by data movement. Good locality reuses nearby or recently accessed data, improving cache hit rates and reducing time spent waiting for slower memory.
Operating systems use process isolation to limit interference between programs. Each process normally receives its own virtual address space and cannot freely read or modify another process's memory.
Isolation does not prevent all interprocess communication. Pipes, sockets, and controlled shared-memory mechanisms allow data exchange while the operating system enforces boundaries and permissions.
Deadlock can occur when several execution units wait for resources held by one another. If the wait relationships form an unbreakable cycle, none of the participants can make progress.
One strategy for preventing deadlock is to enforce a consistent order for acquiring resources. This breaks circular wait but can introduce tradeoffs in performance and programming complexity.
A database transaction groups several operations into one logical unit. A money transfer, for example, should not be considered complete if one account is debited but the other is never credited.

Transaction isolation controls which intermediate states concurrent operations can observe. Stronger isolation often simplifies correctness reasoning but may reduce concurrency or increase coordination cost.

A database index stores an additional structure that helps locate matching records quickly. It can reduce the amount of data scanned, but it also consumes storage and adds work to inserts and updates.
Whether an index is useful depends on the query and data distribution. If a query must read most of a table anyway, a sequential scan can sometimes be more efficient than using an index.

Internet links are shared by many connections. If every sender transmits without restraint, router queues grow and packet loss rises, so congestion-control algorithms adjust sending rates in response to network conditions.
Congestion control differs from flow control. Flow control prevents a sender from overwhelming the receiver, while congestion control responds to excessive load along the network path itself.

Public-key cryptography uses a mathematically related pair of keys, one of which can be shared openly while the other remains secret. It enables secure protocols without requiring every pair of users to share one secret key in advance.

Digital signatures use a private key to create evidence that can be checked with the corresponding public key. A signature authenticates origin and integrity but does not by itself hide the message contents.
A file system organizes persistent storage into files and directories and tracks metadata such as names, permissions, and timestamps. It also records which storage blocks are free or allocated.
Power failure can interrupt a file update partway through. Journaling file systems record critical update information so that they can recover a consistent structure after a crash.

The learning rate controls the size of each parameter update. If it is too large, optimization can overshoot low-loss regions or diverge; if it is too small, training may progress unnecessarily slowly.
Learning-rate schedules often use larger updates early and smaller ones later. Choosing an appropriate learning rate is often more important than simply increasing the number of training epochs.
Weight decay is a common regularization method that discourages parameters from growing without restraint during optimization. It can reduce the tendency to fit narrow details of the training set.
More regularization is not always better. Excessive weight decay can limit model capacity and hurt both training and validation performance, so its strength must be tuned on held-out data.
Dropout randomly masks a subset of intermediate activations during training, preventing the model from relying on exactly the same units for every prediction and providing a regularizing effect.

During inference, activations are normally no longer dropped at random; the full network is used with the appropriate scaling convention. Training and evaluation modes therefore must be handled explicitly.

Early stopping uses validation performance to decide when training should end. If training loss keeps falling while validation loss consistently worsens, further optimization is likely increasing memorization.

Early stopping works best when the checkpoint with the best validation metric is saved, rather than keeping only the final epoch. This allows training to return to parameters with better generalization.
Cross-validation divides data into several disjoint folds and rotates which fold is held out for validation. It can estimate model stability more efficiently when the available dataset is limited.

Cross-validation is mainly a model-selection and estimation tool, not a replacement for a final independent test set. Repeated tuning on cross-validation results still requires a separate final evaluation.
Gradient clipping limits the magnitude of gradients used in an update and can prevent sudden large gradients from destabilizing training. It is common in deep and sequence models.
Gradient clipping does not fix every optimization problem. If the learning rate is inappropriate or the data pipeline is faulty, clipping may only hide the underlying issue.

Batch size determines how many training examples contribute to one parameter update. Small batches produce noisier gradient estimates, while large batches are usually more stable but require more memory.

Changing batch size often requires reconsidering the learning rate. Together they determine how much data contributes to an update and how far parameters move, so the two settings are not independent.
Data encountered after deployment can differ from the training distribution. Changes in users, devices, seasons, or business rules can all create distribution shift.

Strong validation performance applies only to data sufficiently similar to the validation set. Deployed systems still need monitoring for changes in inputs and error patterns that indicate the model is moving outside its original operating regime.

A classifier can have high accuracy while producing poorly calibrated probabilities. Calibration asks whether events assigned a probability such as seventy percent actually occur about seventy percent of the time in the long run.

Probability calibration matters in risk-sensitive decisions. Two models can have similar accuracy while the one with more reliable probabilities is better for thresholding and uncertainty-aware decisions.

Representation learning allows a model to discover useful features from data rather than relying entirely on manually designed inputs. Good representations make task-relevant structure easier for later layers to use.

An internal representation is not necessarily a directly interpretable human concept. Neural vectors can encode several statistical relationships at once, so assigning one fixed meaning to a single dimension can be misleading.

Every measurement has finite precision, so a scientific result should not be treated as an exact number without uncertainty. Measurement uncertainty describes a reasonable range around the reported value under the stated method and conditions.

Repeated measurements help estimate random variation but do not automatically remove systematic bias. If an instrument consistently reads too high, more repetitions will cluster around the wrong center.
A confounder influences both an exposure and an outcome and can create a misleading association between them. Age, for example, may affect both a behavior and a health outcome.

Statistical adjustment can reduce the influence of measured confounders, but it cannot guarantee removal of unknown ones. Causal conclusions from observational data therefore depend on explicit assumptions.
Statistical significance does not imply a large practical effect. An effect size describes the magnitude of a difference or association and helps assess scientific or practical importance.

The same numerical effect size can matter differently across contexts. A small average benefit may still be valuable for a serious condition with low treatment cost, while the same change may be irrelevant elsewhere.

A confidence interval gives a range of parameter values compatible with the sample and modeling assumptions, while also reflecting estimation precision. Larger samples often produce narrower intervals when data quality is maintained.
A narrow interval does not guarantee correctness. Systematic sampling bias can produce a very precise estimate that is still far from the target population value.
Running many statistical tests on the same dataset increases the chance of finding small p-values by accident even when all null hypotheses are true.

Multiple-comparison correction, prespecified primary outcomes, and independent replication can reduce selective discoveries. Reporting only the most significant result while hiding failed analyses gives a distorted picture of evidence.

Replication tests whether a result can be observed again with new samples, times, or laboratories. One successful experiment is evidence, but it cannot establish that an effect is stable in every setting.
A failed replication also requires interpretation. It may indicate an unstable effect, or it may result from different samples, procedures, or measurement precision, so experimental details matter.

A feedback-control system compares a desired target with the measured output and adjusts its input according to the error. Thermostats, drone stabilization, and industrial speed control all use this general idea.
Feedback that is too weak can produce sluggish response, while overly aggressive feedback can cause oscillation or instability. Controller design balances speed, accuracy, and stability.
Sensor readings usually contain noise, so one measurement is not identical to the true state. Filtering combines observations, and sometimes a system model, to produce a more stable estimate.
Filtering cannot be increased without limit because real changes may then be smoothed away as if they were noise. Signal processing must balance responsiveness against stability.
Error-correcting codes add structured redundancy so that a receiver can detect and sometimes repair transmission errors. Redundancy consumes extra bandwidth but improves reliability.
Different codes suit different noise conditions and computational budgets. Communication systems balance code rate, delay, decoding complexity, and residual error probability.
A continuous signal must be sampled in time before digital processing. If the sampling rate is too low, high-frequency variation can appear falsely as a lower frequency, a phenomenon called aliasing.

An analog low-pass filter is often applied before sampling to limit input bandwidth. More powerful digital processing cannot fully recover information that was already lost or aliased during sampling.

Mathematical models trade realism for tractability. A model selects a limited set of variables and represents their relationships with equations, functions, or probability distributions. More complexity is not automatically better, because extra parameters can make estimation unstable and can fit details that do not generalize. A useful model states its assumptions, identifies its operating range, and is tested on observations that were not used to construct it. Approximation is therefore not careless simplification; it is a controlled decision about which structure matters for the question and how much error the omitted detail may introduce.

Computer systems manage complexity through layers of abstraction. An application rarely manipulates transistors directly; it uses programming languages, libraries, operating-system services, and processor instructions. Each layer exposes a simpler interface while hiding many details below it. Abstraction improves productivity, but it can also hide performance costs. A single file-read operation may involve caches, system calls, file-system metadata, and a storage device. Diagnosing performance therefore requires opening the appropriate abstraction layer and measuring the actual bottleneck rather than guessing from surface code.

Preventing overfitting is not the same as preventing training loss from decreasing. The goal is to preserve performance on unseen data.
